name: OBS Traceability - AAP
rows: 02. Entity Protective Security Roles and Responsibilities
A Chief Information Security Officer is appointed to oversee the entity's cyber security program and the cyber security for the entity's most critical technology resources.
CISO oversight is a mandatory governance dependency for A&A because authorisation decisions rely on cyber security leadership over NDIA's cyber program and critical technology resources.
Applicable as PSPF-aligned better practice for NDIA. Applies to NDIA-owned, operated, outsourced and cloud-hosted ICT systems, with priority for critical services and participant-data systems.
Roles and responsibilities — CISO and security governance
NDIA must appoint and maintain a CISO role with authority to oversee the cyber security program, the A&A framework, and the security posture of NDIA's most critical technology resources.
02. Entity Protective Security Roles and Responsibilities
The Chief Information Security Officer is accountable to the Accountable Authority for cyber security risks and how the entity's cyber security program is managing these risks.
A&A decisions require clear accountability for cyber risk and assurance outcomes; PSPF requires the CISO to be accountable to the Accountable Authority for these risks.
Applicable as PSPF-aligned better practice for NDIA. The CISO's A&A risk advice should support decisions by the NDIA Board, CEO and delegated authorising officers.
The NDIA CISO must provide accountable advice to the NDIA Accountable Authority or delegate on cyber security risks, control effectiveness and residual risks accepted through system A&A.
02. Entity Protective Security Roles and Responsibilities
The Accountable Authority approves security governance arrangements that are tailored to the entity's size, complexity and risk environment.
The A&A policy must be approved within NDIA's security governance arrangements so that decision rights, delegations, assurance expectations and escalation paths are enforceable.
Applicable as PSPF-aligned better practice for NDIA. Governance should be tailored to NDIA's scale, participant-data sensitivity, outsourced delivery model and technology complexity.
NDIA's Accountable Authority or approved delegate must endorse ICT A&A governance, including delegations for authorising officers, security assessors, risk acceptance and exceptions.
Risk appetite, ownership and internal control
The Accountable Authority determines their entity's tolerance for security risks and documents in the security plan.
A&A depends on documented risk tolerance because an authorising officer can only accept residual security risk that is within the entity's approved appetite and tolerance.
Applicable as PSPF-aligned better practice for NDIA. Use NDIA's enterprise risk appetite and security plan to determine acceptable residual ICT security risk.
Risk appetite, tolerance and acceptance criteria
ICT systems must not be authorised to operate unless residual security risks are assessed against NDIA's documented risk appetite, security risk tolerance and applicable control baselines.
Risk appetite, ownership and internal control
A risk steward (or manager) is identified for each security risk or category of security risk, including shared risks.
Risk stewardship is required so that every A&A risk has an accountable owner who can treat, monitor and report residual risk during the system lifecycle.
Applicable as PSPF-aligned better practice for NDIA. Each ICT security risk, shared risk and supplier risk should have a named risk owner or steward.
Risk ownership, stewardship and shared-risk management
For each system undergoing A&A, NDIA must identify a system owner and risk steward responsible for security risk treatment, shared-risk coordination and ongoing control assurance.
Risk appetite, ownership and internal control
The Accountable Authority considers the impact that their security risk management decisions could potentially have on other entities, and shares information on risks where appropriate.
ICT authorisation decisions may affect other Commonwealth entities, service providers and participants; shared and downstream security impacts must be considered.
Applicable as PSPF-aligned better practice for NDIA, particularly for shared services, connected systems, inter-agency data exchanges and externally hosted services.
A&A assessments must identify security risks to other entities, connected services, shared platforms and third parties, and require information sharing or escalation where appropriate.

The entity is accountable for the management of security risks arising from procuring goods and services and ensures procurement and contract decisions do not expose the entity or the Australian Government to an unacceptable level of risk.
Supplier and procurement risks can invalidate an A&A decision if unmanaged; the policy must require procurement decisions to avoid unacceptable security risk.
Applicable. NDIA uses ICT suppliers, managed services and cloud services; A&A must include procurement, contractual and third-party security assurance before use.

ICT procurements and service engagements must include security risk assessment and A&A evidence before production use, ensuring supplier arrangements do not create unacceptable NDIA or Commonwealth risk.

Procurement, contracts and third-party outsourced arrangements contain proportionate security terms and conditions to ensure service providers, contractors and subcontractors comply with relevant PSPF Requirements.
A&A outcomes must be supported by enforceable contract terms requiring providers to meet PSPF/ISM and NDIA security obligations.
Applicable. Include in contracts, statements of work and service schedules for NDIA ICT providers, contractors, subcontractors, cloud and managed service providers.
Third-party security clauses and supplier obligations
NDIA ICT contracts must include proportionate security clauses requiring providers and subcontractors to comply with applicable PSPF, ISM, A&A, incident reporting and assurance obligations.
Entity ensures service providers, contractors and subcontractors comply with relevant PSPF Requirements as detailed by the entity.
Authorisation evidence must extend to service providers because outsourced controls remain part of NDIA's system risk profile.
Applicable. Applies to all providers and subcontractors supporting systems in scope of NDIA ICT A&A.
System owners must verify and record that ICT providers and subcontractors comply with NDIA-defined PSPF, ISM, privacy, security and A&A obligations relevant to the system.
Incident response, breach notification and operational readiness

Contractual security terms and conditions require service providers to report any actual or suspected security incidents to the entity, and follow reasonable direction from the entity arising from incident investigations.
Incident reporting obligations are necessary to preserve authorisation, trigger reassessment and support NDIA's response to suspected or actual security compromise.
Applicable. Include in supplier contracts, operational procedures and authorisation conditions for all externally provided ICT systems and services.
Supplier incident reporting and security event escalation
NDIA ICT contracts must require providers to promptly report actual or suspected security incidents and follow NDIA directions for investigation, containment, remediation and A&A reassessment.
Cloud, hosting, data centres, gateways and shared responsibility
Government entities providing outsourced services provide IRAP assessment reports to the government entities consuming, or looking to consume, their services.
IRAP assessment reports are key assurance evidence for outsourced government services and cloud services considered during A&A.
Applicable where NDIA consumes government-provided outsourced services, cloud services or managed platforms that provide IRAP reports.

Where an outsourced government or cloud service is consumed, the system owner must obtain and assess relevant IRAP reports and record inherited controls, residual risks and approval conditions in the A&A package.

Contract security terms and conditions are monitored and reviewed to ensure the specified security controls, terms and conditions are implemented, operated and maintained by the contracted provider, including any subcontractors, over the life of a contract.
Contractual controls must be monitored after ATO because authorisation is not a one-off event and supplier control failure can change residual risk.
Applicable. Applies for the life of NDIA ICT contracts supporting authorised systems and services.
Ongoing supplier assurance and contract monitoring

System owners must monitor contracted security controls, assurance commitments and subcontractor obligations for authorised systems throughout the contract lifecycle and escalate non-compliance for risk review.
Contractual terms and conditions include appropriate security arrangements for the completion or termination of the contract.
Completion or termination of contracts can expose information, credentials, assets and residual access; A&A must require secure transition and offboarding controls.
Applicable. Applies to NDIA ICT contracts, cloud exits, managed-service transitions and supplier offboarding.
Secure transition, exit and termination controls

NDIA ICT contracts must define secure transition and termination requirements, including return or destruction of information, access revocation, asset sanitisation and evidence required before A&A closure.
Procurement and contract decisions consider the security risks before engaging providers operating under foreign ownership, control or influence.
Foreign ownership, control or influence can materially affect supplier and system risk; A&A must require this risk to be assessed before engagement and during service delivery.
Applicable. Applies to NDIA procurement and ongoing assurance for ICT suppliers, cloud providers and managed service providers.
Foreign ownership, control or influence risk assessment

A&A and procurement processes must assess and document supplier foreign ownership, control or influence risks and require CISO or delegate approval of residual risk before engagement or continued use.
Security risks arising from contractual arrangements for the provision of goods and services are managed, reassessed and adjusted over the life of a contract.
A&A must remain current over the contract lifecycle because supplier risk, threat conditions and service architecture can change.
Applicable. Applies to all NDIA ICT systems and services delivered under contract or supplier arrangements.
Supplier lifecycle risk review and reauthorisation triggers
Supplier-related security risks must be reassessed during the contract lifecycle, including at renewal, major change, incident, material subcontractor change or when residual risk exceeds tolerance.
Secure and verifiable third-party vendors, providers, partners and associated services are used unless business operations require use, and the residual risks are managed and approved by the CISO.
Use of unverifiable or insecure third parties can undermine ATO; residual risk requires CISO visibility and approval when business need requires use.
Applicable. Applies to all third-party technologies, integrations, SaaS, managed services and associated services used by NDIA.
Third-party assurance, exceptions and CISO approval

NDIA must use secure and verifiable third-party vendors wherever practicable; any exception must have documented business justification, residual risk treatment and CISO approval before authorisation.
System definition, boundary, classification and criticality

The value, importance or sensitivity of official information is assessed by the originator by considering the potential damage to the government, the national interest, organisations or individuals that would arise if the information's confidentiality were compromised.
System security categorisation and control selection depend on the assessed value, sensitivity and confidentiality impact of information processed by the system.
Applicable. Applies to NDIA systems that process participant, operational, corporate, official or security classified information.
Information classification and system security categorisation

Before A&A, system owners must identify information types, sensitivity, confidentiality impact, business impact level and protective marking requirements that drive the system's security categorisation.
Records, metadata, retention and secure disposal

The Australian Government Recordkeeping Metadata Standard's 'Security Classification' property (and where relevant, the 'Security Caveat' property) is applied to protectively mark information on technology systems that store, process or communicate security classified information.
Security classification and caveat metadata must be reflected in systems that store, process or communicate classified information to support handling, access and audit controls.
Conditional. Applies where NDIA systems store, process or communicate security classified information, and as good practice for metadata-enabled information management.
Metadata, labelling and protective marking controls
Systems in scope of A&A must support required security classification and caveat metadata, including Australian Government Recordkeeping Metadata Standard fields where applicable.
Records, metadata, retention and secure disposal
Apply the Australian Government Recordkeeping Metadata Standard's 'Rights' property where the entity wishes to categorise information content by the type of restrictions on access.
Rights metadata supports access restrictions and need-to-know controls, which are core A&A considerations for systems holding sensitive or restricted information.
Applicable where NDIA categorises information by access restrictions or business rules; especially relevant for participant data and sensitive operational records.
Access restriction metadata and information rights
A&A evidence must confirm that systems requiring content-level access restrictions can apply and preserve appropriate Rights metadata or equivalent access-control attributes.
System definition, boundary, classification and criticality
Entity implements operational controls for its information holdings that are proportional to their value, importance and sensitivity.
Operational controls must be proportionate to the information's value, importance and sensitivity, which directly determines the authorisation baseline.
Applicable. Applies to all NDIA information holdings and supporting ICT systems, with stronger controls for high-value, sensitive or critical data.
Information holdings, aggregation risk and control proportionality
System A&A must assess information holdings, aggregation risk and business impact, then require operational controls proportionate to the information's value, importance and sensitivity.
Baseline security controls and access safeguards
The Australian Signals Directorate's Information Security Manual cyber security principles are applied during all stages of the lifecycle of each system.
ISM cyber security principles are the foundation for secure lifecycle management and must be applied during design, build, change, operation and disposal.
Applicable. Applies to all NDIA ICT systems and technology lifecycle stages, including new projects, major changes, cloud services and decommissioning.
NDIA ICT systems must apply ASD ISM cyber security principles throughout the technology lifecycle and record how the principles are addressed in A&A artefacts.
Baseline security controls and access safeguards
The Australian Signals Directorate's Information Security Manual controls and cyber security guidelines are applied on a risk-based approach.
Risk-based application of ISM controls is central to system assessment, control selection and residual-risk acceptance before an ATO decision.
Applicable. Applies to all NDIA systems, with scope and depth scaled by classification, business impact, threat exposure and criticality.
Security control framework — ISM controls and guidelines
A&A packages must map applicable ISM controls and guidelines to the system context, document implementation status, inherited controls, gaps, risk treatments and accepted residual risks.
System definition, boundary, classification and criticality

A Technology Asset Stocktake and Technology Security Risk Management Plan is created to identify and manage the entity's internet-facing systems or services to ensure continuous visibility and monitoring of the entity's resource and technology estate.
A technology asset stocktake and risk management plan provide the inventory and risk context required for A&A scope, monitoring and continuous visibility.
Applicable. Applies to NDIA's technology estate, especially internet-facing systems, services, software, platforms and infrastructure used to deliver NDIS functions.
Technology asset stocktake and technology security risk management plan

NDIA must maintain technology asset stocktake and security risk management artefacts that identify internet-facing systems and services, owners, criticality, authorisation status and monitoring obligations.
ISM-aligned A&A lifecycle and authorisation decision

The Authorising Officer authorises each technology system to operate based on the acceptance of the residual security risks associated with its operation before that system processes, stores or communicates government information or data.
This is the core A&A requirement: systems must be authorised to operate based on accepted residual security risk before handling government information or data.
Directly applicable. Applies to every NDIA ICT system before production operation, including new systems, material changes, externally hosted services and cloud platforms.
Authority to Operate decision and residual-risk acceptance
No NDIA ICT system may process, store or communicate government information or data in production until an authorised officer has accepted residual security risk and granted authority to operate.
ISM-aligned A&A lifecycle and authorisation decision
Decisions to authorise (or reauthorise) a new technology system or make changes to an existing technology system are based on the ISM's risk-based approach to cyber security.
Authorisation and reauthorisation must follow the ISM's risk-based approach so that decisions are evidence-based and tailored to system risk.
Directly applicable. Applies to new NDIA systems, major releases, architecture changes, cloud onboarding and security-impacting changes.
A&A lifecycle — assessment, authorisation and reauthorisation
Decisions to authorise or reauthorise systems must use an ISM-aligned risk assessment, control assurance evidence, threat context and documented residual-risk acceptance.
System definition, boundary, classification and criticality
The technology system is authorised to the highest security classification of the information and data it will process, store or communicate.
Authorising to the highest classification ensures the system's approved operating boundary matches the most sensitive information it can process.
Directly applicable where systems handle classified information; for unclassified systems, use OFFICIAL/OFFICIAL: Sensitive and business impact categorisation to set control baselines.
Security categorisation and approved operating classification
Each system's ATO must state the maximum approved security classification, sensitivity, business impact level and data types the system may process, store or communicate.
ISM-aligned A&A lifecycle and authorisation decision

A register of the entity's authorised technology systems is developed, implemented and maintained, and includes the name and position of the Authorising Officer, system owner, date of authorisation, and any decisions to accept residual security risks.
A register of authorised systems is required to evidence ATO status, decision owners, dates and accepted residual risks.
Directly applicable. NDIA should maintain a central register for all authorised ICT systems and services, including inherited and externally hosted services.
Authorised systems register and residual-risk record
NDIA must maintain a register of authorised ICT systems recording system owner, authorising officer, authorisation date, scope, expiry or review triggers and residual-risk decisions.

Each technology system's suitability to be authorised to operate is reassessed when it undergoes significant functionality or architectural change, or where the system's security environment has changed considerably.
Reassessment triggers keep authorisation valid when functionality, architecture, threats or security environment changes materially.
Directly applicable. Applies to NDIA system changes, cloud service changes, supplier changes, major incidents, vulnerability exposure and threat-environment shifts.
System suitability for continued operation must be reassessed after significant functional, architectural, supplier, threat or security-environment change, or when residual risk exceeds tolerance.
Risk appetite, ownership and internal control
The Australian Signals Directorate's temporary mitigations for legacy IT are applied to manage legacy information technology that cannot yet be replaced.
Legacy technology can create unacceptable residual risk unless temporary mitigations and treatment plans are applied and monitored.
Applicable where NDIA retains legacy IT that cannot yet be replaced or upgraded.
Legacy technology, compensating controls and risk treatment
Legacy technology may only remain authorised where ASD temporary mitigations, compensating controls, risk treatment plans and time-bound remediation actions are documented and approved.
Physical security and facility accreditation dependencies
Technology assets and their components, classified as SECRET or below are stored in the appropriate Security Zone based on their aggregated security classification or business impact level.
Physical storage of technology assets affects confidentiality, integrity and availability and is a dependency for secure system operation.
Conditional. Applies where NDIA stores technology assets or components that are SECRET or below, or where aggregated holdings drive a higher business impact level.
Technology asset hosting, storage and physical-security dependencies
A&A must confirm that technology assets and components are stored in security zones appropriate to their classification, aggregation and business impact level before authorisation.
Physical security and facility accreditation dependencies
Technology assets and their components classified as TOP SECRET are stored in suitable SCEC-endorsed racks or compartments within an accredited Security Zone Five area.
TOP SECRET technology assets require highly controlled storage; the policy should include a conditional requirement to prevent accidental non-compliance.
Conditional. Applies only if NDIA handles TOP SECRET technology assets or components.
TOP SECRET technology asset storage dependencies
Where a system or component is TOP SECRET, A&A must require suitable SCEC-endorsed racks or compartments within an accredited Security Zone Five area before operational use.
Physical security and facility accreditation dependencies

Outsourced facilities that house technology assets and their components with a catastrophic business impact level are certified by ASIO T4 physical security and accredited by ASD before they are used operationally.
Facilities that house catastrophic-impact technology assets must be certified and accredited before use, as facility risk forms part of system residual risk.
Conditional. Applies where NDIA uses outsourced facilities for technology assets or components with catastrophic business impact level.
Outsourced facility assurance for high-impact systems
A&A for high-impact outsourced hosting facilities must include evidence of required ASIO T4 physical security certification and ASD accreditation before operational use.
Records, metadata, retention and secure disposal
Technology assets are disposed of securely in accordance with the Information Security Manual.
Secure disposal is a lifecycle control that must be planned in A&A to prevent data leakage, credential exposure and unauthorised recovery of technology assets.
Applicable. Applies to all NDIA ICT assets, media, devices, cloud resources and system components at decommissioning or disposal.
A&A closure and decommissioning must require secure disposal, sanitisation or destruction of technology assets and data in accordance with the ISM and NDIA records obligations.
Baseline security controls and access safeguards
Approved post-quantum cryptographic encryption algorithms are used for newly procured cryptographic equipment and software in accordance with the ISM's guidelines for cryptography.
Cryptographic choices are part of the system security baseline; new procurements must support approved post-quantum algorithms where required.
Applicable to new NDIA cryptographic equipment, software and services, and to procurement or refresh decisions involving encryption.
New cryptographic equipment and software must use approved algorithms, including post-quantum cryptographic requirements where applicable, and record cryptographic design decisions in A&A evidence.

A cyber security strategy and uplift plan is developed, implemented and maintained to manage the entity's cyber security risks in accordance with the ISM and the Guiding Principles to Embed a Zero Trust Culture.
A&A must align to the entity's cyber security strategy and uplift plan so system-level risk treatment contributes to enterprise risk reduction.
Applicable. NDIA system authorisation should align with cyber strategy, uplift priorities, zero trust principles and ISM implementation.
Cyber security strategy alignment and uplift planning
ICT A&A must align system risk treatments, control uplift and exceptions with NDIA's cyber security strategy, uplift plan, ISM obligations and zero trust objectives.
The CISO reports on the entity's cyber security risk at each meeting of the Audit Committee and biannually on the progress of the cyber security strategy and uplift plan.
Regular CISO cyber-risk reporting supports governance oversight of authorisation status, residual risks, exceptions and uplift progress.
Applicable. A&A reporting should feed NDIA Board or audit/risk committee oversight and executive cyber risk reporting.
A&A reporting, metrics and governance oversight
The CISO must report material A&A risks, authorisation status, overdue reassessments, control gaps and cyber uplift progress through NDIA's audit/risk governance processes.
Baseline security controls and access safeguards
Patch applications mitigation strategy is implemented to Maturity Level Two under ASD's Essential Eight Maturity Model.
Patch application maturity is a mandatory control baseline that materially affects whether a system can be authorised or remain authorised.
Applicable. Applies to NDIA systems, applications, SaaS configurations and supporting technology within A&A scope.
A&A must verify that application patching meets at least ASD Essential Eight Maturity Level Two or has approved, documented compensating controls and risk acceptance.
Baseline security controls and access safeguards
Patch operating systems mitigation strategy is implemented to Maturity Level Two under ASD's Essential Eight Maturity Model.
Operating system patching reduces exploitable vulnerabilities and is a minimum cyber control considered during authorisation.
Applicable. Applies to NDIA-managed servers, endpoints, appliances, cloud workloads and managed service environments as relevant.
Essential Eight baseline — patch operating systems
A&A must verify that operating system patching meets at least ASD Essential Eight Maturity Level Two or has approved, documented compensating controls and remediation timeframes.
Baseline security controls and access safeguards
Multi-factor authentication mitigation strategy is implemented to Maturity Level Two under ASD's Essential Eight Maturity Model.
Multi-factor authentication is a minimum control for reducing identity compromise and must be considered before granting access to authorised systems.
Applicable. Applies to privileged, user, remote, cloud, administrative and third-party access to NDIA systems.
A&A must verify that MFA meets at least ASD Essential Eight Maturity Level Two for applicable user, privileged, remote and administrative access pathways.
Baseline security controls and access safeguards
Restrict administrative privileges mitigation strategy is implemented to Maturity Level Two under ASD's Essential Eight Maturity Model.
Administrative privilege restrictions are critical for limiting compromise impact and must be evidenced during A&A.
Applicable. Applies to NDIA privileged accounts, service accounts, administrators, support providers and cloud administrators.
Essential Eight baseline — restrict administrative privileges
A&A must verify that administrative privileges are restricted, justified, reviewed, monitored and implemented to at least ASD Essential Eight Maturity Level Two.
Baseline security controls and access safeguards
Application control mitigation strategy is implemented to Maturity Level Two under ASD's Essential Eight Maturity Model.
Application control prevents unauthorised code execution and is a minimum control for reducing malware and unauthorised software risk.
Applicable. Applies to NDIA endpoints, servers and workloads where application control is relevant and technically feasible.
A&A must verify that application control is implemented to at least ASD Essential Eight Maturity Level Two, or document approved scope limitations and compensating controls.
Baseline security controls and access safeguards
Restrict Microsoft Office macros mitigation strategy is implemented to Maturity Level Two under ASD's Essential Eight Maturity Model.
Macro restrictions reduce common malware delivery risk and form part of the mandatory cyber control baseline.
Applicable. Applies to NDIA desktop, productivity and collaboration environments and any system enabling macro-capable files.
Essential Eight baseline — restrict Microsoft Office macros
A&A must verify that Microsoft Office macro controls meet at least ASD Essential Eight Maturity Level Two, with exceptions documented and approved.
Baseline security controls and access safeguards
User application hardening mitigation strategy is implemented to Maturity Level Two under ASD's Essential Eight Maturity Model.
User application hardening reduces exposure through browsers, document readers and common user applications that interact with NDIA systems.
Applicable. Applies to NDIA user environments, standard operating environments and application platforms within A&A scope.
Essential Eight baseline — user application hardening
A&A must verify that user application hardening meets at least ASD Essential Eight Maturity Level Two for relevant user environments and system access paths.
Baseline security controls and access safeguards
Regular back-ups mitigation strategy is implemented to Maturity Level Two under ASD's Essential Eight Maturity Model.
Regular backups are necessary for availability, recovery and resilience and are part of the minimum authorisation control baseline.
Applicable. Applies to NDIA systems and data sets requiring backup, restoration, disaster recovery or service continuity capability.
A&A must verify that backup and restoration controls meet at least ASD Essential Eight Maturity Level Two and that restoration evidence supports operational resilience requirements.
Baseline security controls and access safeguards

The remaining mitigation strategies from the Strategies to Mitigate Cyber Security Incidents are considered and, where required, implemented to achieve an acceptable level of residual risk for their entity.
The Essential Eight is not sufficient for all threats; the policy must require additional strategies where residual risk warrants them.
Applicable. Applies to all NDIA A&A decisions, especially high-risk, internet-facing, sensitive, critical or third-party integrated systems.
Additional cyber mitigation strategies and residual-risk treatment
Where Essential Eight controls do not reduce risk to tolerance, A&A must require additional mitigation strategies from ASD guidance and document the resulting treatment plan.
Baseline security controls and access safeguards
A Protective Domain Name System service or other security mechanisms is used to prevent connections to and from known malicious endpoints.
Protective DNS or equivalent controls reduce connections to known malicious infrastructure and support authorisation of internet-connected services.
Applicable. Applies to NDIA internet-connected systems, endpoints, networks, gateways and cloud environments where DNS or equivalent controls are available.
A&A for internet-connected systems must verify use of Protective DNS or equivalent controls to block or detect connections to known malicious endpoints.
Cloud, hosting, data centres, gateways and shared responsibility
Cloud Service Providers that have completed an IRAP assessment against the latest version of ASD's ISM within the previous 24 months are used.
Recent IRAP assessment evidence is required for cloud provider assurance and is a key input to cloud system authorisation.
Applicable where NDIA uses cloud service providers or cloud services for systems in A&A scope.
NDIA must use cloud services supported by an IRAP assessment against the latest ISM within the previous 24 months, unless an approved exception and risk treatment is documented.
Security testing, vulnerability management and remediation
Entities consider IRAP assessment recommendations and findings, and implement on a risk-based approach.
IRAP findings and recommendations must be evaluated, not merely collected, because they determine inherited controls, gaps and residual risks.
Applicable where NDIA consumes cloud, gateway, managed service or outsourced services with IRAP reports.
IRAP findings review and treatment planning
System owners must review IRAP findings, document applicability to NDIA's configuration and data, treat relevant risks, and record accepted residual risks in the A&A package.
Cloud, hosting, data centres, gateways and shared responsibility

Security classified or systems of government significance information and data is securely hosted using a Cloud Service Provider and Data Centre Provider that has been certified against the Australian Government Hosting Certification Framework.
Hosting certification affects the assurance of classified and systems-of-government-significance information and must be captured before authorisation.
Conditional. Applies where NDIA hosts security classified information or a system declared as a System of Government Significance.
Certified hosting and data centre assurance
A&A must verify that hosting for security classified or declared SOGS information uses appropriately certified cloud and data centre providers before operational approval.
Cloud, hosting, data centres, gateways and shared responsibility
The Data Centre Facilities Supplies Panel is used when procuring certified data centre space and services.
Use of certified data centre arrangements supports facility and supply-chain assurance for systems with hosting requirements.
Conditional. Applies where NDIA procures certified data centre space or services for ICT systems in scope.
Data centre procurement and facilities assurance
Where certified data centre services are required, NDIA procurement and A&A must use the Data Centre Facilities Supplies Panel or approved equivalent arrangement.
Cloud, hosting, data centres, gateways and shared responsibility
Internet-connected technology systems, and the data they process, store or communicate, are protected by a gateway in accordance with the ISM and the Gateways Policy.
Gateways are boundary controls that protect internet-connected systems and must be verified before authorising systems that connect to external networks.
Applicable. Applies to NDIA internet-connected technology systems and data flows.
Gateway, boundary and internet connection controls
A&A must verify that internet-connected systems and their data flows are protected by gateways or equivalent controls in accordance with the ISM and applicable gateway policy.
Cloud, hosting, data centres, gateways and shared responsibility

Digital Infrastructure that processes, stores or communicates Australian Government security classified information is protected by a Gateway or Security Service Edge in accordance with the Australian Government Gateway Security Standard.
Digital infrastructure handling security classified information requires gateway or SSE protections aligned to the Australian Government Gateway Security Standard.
Conditional. Applies where NDIA digital infrastructure processes, stores or communicates Australian Government security classified information.
Gateway or Secure Service Edge controls for classified digital infrastructure

Digital infrastructure handling security classified information must be protected by a Gateway or Secure Service Edge aligned with the Australian Government Gateway Security Standard before authorisation.
Cloud, hosting, data centres, gateways and shared responsibility
Gateways or Secure Service Edges that have completed an IRAP assessment (or ASD assessment for TOP SECRET gateways) against the latest version of ASD's ISM within the previous 24 months are used.
Gateways and SSEs are high-value boundary controls; recent IRAP or ASD assessment evidence is required before relying on them for A&A.
Applicable where NDIA uses gateways or Secure Service Edges; TOP SECRET use requires ASD assessment.
A&A must require evidence that Gateways or Secure Service Edges have current IRAP assessment, or ASD assessment for TOP SECRET gateways, before they are relied on for system authorisation.
Security testing, vulnerability management and remediation
A vulnerability disclosure program and supporting processes and procedures are established to receive, verify, resolve and report on vulnerabilities disclosed by both internal and external sources.
A vulnerability disclosure process ensures external and internal vulnerability reports can trigger triage, remediation and A&A risk review.
Applicable. Applies to NDIA internet-facing systems, public digital services, software products, APIs and managed services.
Vulnerability disclosure, remediation and authorisation triggers
NDIA must maintain vulnerability disclosure and triage processes, and system owners must reassess A&A risk where vulnerabilities materially affect the authorised security posture.
Participate in the Australian Signals Directorate's Cyber Security Partnership Program and notify ASD in the event of a change in the entity's risk profile.
ASD partnership supports threat intelligence sharing and situational awareness that inform ongoing authorisation and risk reassessment.
Applicable. Applies to NDIA cyber security operations and A&A monitoring for material changes to risk profile.
External cyber partnerships and threat intelligence
NDIA must participate in ASD's Cyber Security Partnership Program as required and use threat intelligence to inform A&A reassessment, risk treatment and security uplift priorities.
Conditional SOCI, SOGS and critical infrastructure obligations
Declared Systems of Government Significance are protected in accordance with the Australian Government Systems of Government Significance Standard.
Declared Systems of Government Significance have additional mandatory obligations that must be embedded in authorisation conditions and assurance evidence.
Conditional. Applies only if an NDIA system or service is declared a System of Government Significance.
Systems of Government Significance — enhanced obligations
If an NDIA system is declared a System of Government Significance, its A&A must incorporate the Australian Government SOGS Standard and require evidence of compliance before operation.
Baseline security controls and access safeguards
Appropriate access to official information is enabled, including controlling access (including remote access) to supporting technology systems, networks, infrastructure, devices and applications.
Access controls are fundamental to authorisation because systems must limit access to official information and supporting technology resources.
Applicable. Applies to NDIA systems, networks, infrastructure, devices, applications and remote access pathways.
Access control, authorisation and remote access
A&A must verify that access to official information and supporting technology is controlled, approved, monitored and periodically reviewed in line with least privilege and need-to-know.
Baseline security controls and access safeguards

A unique user identification, authentication and authorisation practice is implemented on each occasion where system access is granted, to manage access to systems holding security classified information.
Unique identification, authentication and authorisation are required to ensure accountable access to systems holding security classified information.
Applicable for systems holding security classified information; good practice for all NDIA systems holding sensitive participant or operational information.
Identity, authentication and privileged access controls
Systems must use unique user identification, authentication and authorisation practices for each access grant, with stronger controls for privileged, remote and classified access.
Physical security and facility accreditation dependencies
Approval for remote access to TOP SECRET information, data or systems in international locations is only granted if approved by the Australian Signals Directorate.
Remote access to TOP SECRET information introduces exceptional risk and requires ASD approval; the A&A policy should include a conditional prohibition and approval gate.

PGPA Act s 5 - Objects of the Act

The Act establishes a coherent system of governance and accountability across Commonwealth entities and requires high standards of governance, performance, accountability and proper use and management of public resources.
ATO and residual risk acceptance are governance/accountability decisions affecting public resources and service delivery.
Statutory mandatory. Applies to NDIA under the NDIS Act and PGPA framework.
ICT A&A decisions must support proper use of public resources and high standards of governance, performance and accountability.
PGPA Act s 15 - Duty to govern the Commonwealth entity
The accountable authority must govern the entity in a way that promotes proper use and management of public resources, achievement of entity purposes and financial sustainability.

Disposal of Commonwealth records, including data and datasets, can occur only if approved by National Archives, required by another law, or a normal administrative practice not disapproved by Archives.
Destruction, de-identification and system decommissioning decisions must be lawful.

No system data, logs or A&A records may be destroyed unless disposal is authorised under an approved records authority, another law or normal administrative practice.

Agencies should create and maintain full and accurate records of their business and implement policies and procedures for records management.

CDR Supplementary Accreditation Guidelines - Mandatory controls

An accredited person must implement the mandatory information security controls in Schedule 2 Part 2 across the CDR data environment; applicants must demonstrate the ability to meet all control requirements.
The scope references CDR testing. These requirements are mandatory where the system is part of the CDR ecosystem.
Conditional. Applies only if NDIA becomes a CDR participant, handles CDR data, integrates with CDR services or is otherwise subject to CDR obligations.

Certain logs and control information must be retained for six years, with 90 days readily accessible.
Affects evidence retention, monitoring and incident investigation for CDR systems.
Conditional for NDIA systems subject to CDR.
CDR systems must retain required logs and control information for the prescribed period and make recent logs readily accessible.
CDR Supplementary Accreditation Guidelines - Third-party responsibility
An accredited person remains responsible for obligations even when using third-party infrastructure and is liable for outsourced service provider handling of CDR data.
Directly supports shared responsibility and cloud/supplier assurance.
Conditional for NDIA CDR systems using cloud, SaaS, managed services or outsourced providers.

CDR Supplementary Accreditation Guidelines - Outsourced control assessment
Controls performed by third-party providers must be assessed and aligned with the CDR information security requirements.

Conditional for NDIA CDR systems with outsourced or inherited controls.

CDR Supplementary Accreditation Guidelines - Define and document the CDR data environment

Applicants/accredited persons must assess, define and document people, processes, technology and controls forming the CDR data environment, including third-party infrastructure and data flows or a written description reviewed by a qualified independent auditor.

CDR Supplementary Accreditation Guidelines - Testing frequency and deficiency reporting
Testing frequency must be specified and control deficiencies must be reported to senior management.
Supports pre-production and ongoing assurance requirements.
CDR systems must have a documented testing schedule and report control deficiencies to senior management with remediation tracking.
CDR Supplementary Accreditation Guidelines - Incident response notifications
Incident response plans must include notification procedures for OAIC, CDR consumers and ACSC within required timeframes for notifiable security incidents.
CDR systems require incident readiness before production use.
CDR systems must include CDR-specific incident notification roles, timeframes and evidence requirements in the CSIRP.

The CDR conformance approach describes mandatory and voluntary activities across development/testing, activation and ongoing conformance.

Conditional for NDIA systems that must conform to CDR participant obligations.
Before activation, CDR systems must complete required conformance activities and retain evidence for ATO.

Participant testing should include unit, system, integration, user acceptance, performance, penetration and secondary data holder testing before the ACCC Conformance Test Suite.

CDR systems must complete internal and security testing, including penetration testing where required, before conformance testing and production activation.
CDR Participant Conformance Approach - CTS completion before active status
Each new participant must complete the Conformance Test Suite before becoming active on the CDR Register.

The CTS is not a full compliance validation; participants remain accountable for compliance with CDR standards and must fix alignment issues before CTS.
